Two important aspects of this theory, work and power, are concerned with two special types of energy, potential and kinetic energy.

When a force affects the motion of an object moving in the direction of an applied force, we can say that work is done.
DISCUSSION
The most important element of force is motion: for work to actually be done, the object must move from one place to another.
For example, no matter how long you hold a heavy load on your shoulders, you are not doing any work on the load.
In reality, you are only exerting an upward force in an attempt to counteract the downward force of gravity on the load.
To get any work done, the load must move. If you raise the load over your head you have done work.
In this example, a force has been exerted which has a component in the direction in which the object moves.

In the examples we've looked at so far, the forces and distances involved did not vary, they remained constant and uniform.
However, forces may vary either in direction or in magnitude (or both) during the time they are acting on an object.
For example, when a force is used to stretch a spring, the magnitude of the force increases as the spring gets longer.
One way to find the amount of work done by a varying force is by a graph having displacement (s) as the x-axis coordinates and force (F) as the y-axis coordinates.
If the force of a spring is uniformly increasing in the direction of the stretching, we can determine the total amount of work that has been exerted.
The force required to stretch a spring depends upon how stiff it is, but the force is always directly proportional to the amount of stretching.
By plotting the values for force and distance on the graph, we can find the total amount of work done by finding the area of the triangle created by the inserted values.
To find the area of the triangle, multiply one half times the product of the base and altitude.
The base of this base is 2.5 meters. The altitude of the triangle is 11 Newtons. Taking one half of this product gives us the total work done, 13.75 Joules.

Like the term "work'', the term "power'' has a scientific meaning much different than its everyday meaning.
DISCUSSION
When we say a person has great power, we usually mean he/she has great strength, or he/she wields great authority.
In science, the term "power'' is much different. Power is defined as the time rate of doing work.
Time considerations are normally not involved in the definition of work.

Also, the same amount of work is done whether you climb a flight of stairs in one minute or five minutes.

Often, we need to know how quickly or slowly work is done. Measurements of power are most commonly used in mechanics and electronics.
To accurately define power, three factors must be taken into consideration.
The displacement of the object, the force in the direction of the displacement, and the time required all combine to describe an object's power.
Since power is the time rate of doing work, we can define it using the following equation: P = W/t where P represents power, W represents work and t is time.
When work equals the product of the force (F) of the object and the object's displacement (s), this equation can also be stated like this:
When work is measured in Joules and time is measured in seconds, power is expressed in Watts (W).
The watt, which is named in honor of the physicist James Watt, is defined as one joule per second. Work
When work is measured in the British system's foot pounds, the unit of power is the foot pounds per second.
A larger unit, known as horsepower (hp), is also used to measure power:
1 hp = 550 ft - lbs/sec = 33,000 ft - lbs/min
This means that a 1 horsepower motor running at full load does 33,000 foot pounds of work every minute.
Since the metric watt is much more common, let's look at some examples of power using the watt.
Since the standard watt is an inconveniently small unit, power is more commonly measured in units of 1000 watts, called kilowatts (kw).

Watts are derived from several different units of measurement. Meters, kilograms, seconds, newtons, and joules all combine together to make up the watt.

The watt is a familiar unit of electrical power; a 100 watt light bulb converts 100 joules of electrical energy into light and heat per second.
The watt does not have to be an electrical unit, though; a light bulb could be rated in horsepower.
Also, some automobile makers rate their engines in kilowatts rather than the standard horsepower.
Power units can be used to define new units of work or energy. For example, the kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the standard unit for measuring the electricity in our homes.
A kilowatt-hour is the total work done in 1 hour (3600 sec) when the power is 1 kw. This means:
It is very important to remember that the kilowatt-hour is a unit of work or energy, not power. You can see this by the way the units cancel each other out.
Although energy, work, and power are abstract physical quantities, they still can be bought and sold.
Although we can't buy a newton of force or a meter per second of velocity, a kilowatt-hour of energy usually costs from two to ten cents, depending on the location and the amount purchased.
For example, if a house consumes 325 kilowatt hours of power (actually, energy) in a week, and the rate is 8 cents per kilowatt, we can determine what the month's power bill will be.
By multiplying the rate times the total number of kilowatt hours used in a week, we have the total cost of electricity for a week.
